opus-5.5.text:
Well, the Microsoft partnership has been really important for us, and I think it's a good example of how we think about partnerships more generally.

When we started Databricks, we were very clear that we wanted to be a multi-cloud company. Customers don't want to be locked into one provider, and data in particular tends to live in many places. So from early on, the question was: how do we work well with each of the major clouds, rather than betting everything on one?

What made Microsoft different is that they were willing to go deeper than a typical marketplace listing. Azure Databricks became a first-party service. It's integrated with their identity, billing, and security, and their sales teams can sell it as part of the Azure offering. For a lot of enterprise customers, that matters. If you're a large bank or a retailer that has already standardized on Azure, being able to adopt Databricks without a separate procurement process or security review removes a lot of friction.

More broadly, I'd say our strategy is to meet customers where they are. We work closely with AWS and Google Cloud as well, and with a wide ecosystem of partners, including system integrators, BI tools, and data providers. The common thread is openness. We built on open source from the beginning: Spark, then Delta Lake, MLflow, and others. That makes partnering easier, because partners aren't worried that we're trying to trap their customers in something proprietary.

Of course, partnerships with cloud providers are always a bit nuanced, because in some areas you cooperate and in others you compete. But I think that's fine. If you focus on giving customers real value, and the partner also benefits, because customers consume more compute and storage on their cloud, then the incentives line up well enough for both sides to invest.

So I'd describe Microsoft as one of our deepest partnerships, but it fits a broader philosophy: be open, be multi-cloud, and integrate deeply wherever that makes life easier for customers.

r001.rationale: The response presents Microsoft as one of Databricks’ deepest partnerships that fits its broader philosophy, describing that strategy as dating back to the company’s start.

r002.rationale: It says Databricks built on open source, including Spark, but does not state an aim to make Spark the de facto standard for data processing.

r003.rationale: It does not say Databricks aimed to be the best place to run Spark.

r004.rationale: It discusses openness and cooperation alongside competition, but does not say Databricks prioritized growing the Spark ecosystem over avoiding partnerships with potential competitors.

r005.rationale: It describes Azure integrations but does not mention a substantial engineering commitment by Databricks to realize the Microsoft partnership.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Microsoft partnership is actually a good lens for how we think about partnerships in general, because it goes back to something that's been true for us from day one. Databricks started with Spark, which is open source, and the whole premise was that you want to meet the customers where they are. Their data is in a particular cloud, their workloads are in a particular cloud, and they don't want to move it. So very early on we decided we were going to be multi-cloud, and that we were not going to compete with the cloud providers on the infrastructure layer. We were going to be the platform that runs on top of it.

Now, Microsoft was really the first one to lean into that in a deep way. Azure Databricks is a first-party service on Azure, which is pretty unusual. It's sold by Microsoft, it's integrated into their billing, their identity, their security model. And I think that happened because we were aligned on what the customer wanted. Microsoft wanted to get enterprise data workloads onto Azure, and we had a product that enterprises wanted for exactly those workloads. So it wasn't a case of two companies deciding to be friends. It was the incentives lining up.

And the way I think about partnerships more broadly is you have to be very honest about where you're complementary and where you overlap. With the cloud providers, there's always some overlap. Microsoft has Fabric and Synapse, Amazon has Redshift and EMR, Google has BigQuery. We compete with all of those products in some accounts. But the overlap is at the margin, and the complementarity is at the core, because the clouds make money when compute runs, and we drive a lot of compute. As long as that's true, the partnership is stable, even when the sales teams occasionally bump into each other.

The other thing I'd say is that the strategy has evolved from being about infrastructure to being about the data and AI ecosystem. Today the partnerships that matter are not just the clouds. It's the model providers, it's the system integrators, it's the ISVs that build on top of the lakehouse. And the principle is the same: open formats, open interfaces, and don't lock the customer in. If you do that, partners want to build on you, because they know you're not going to pull the rug out from under them. The Microsoft relationship was really the first proof point that this approach could work at scale, and we've basically tried to replicate that model everywhere else.

r001.rationale: The response presents Microsoft as an early proof point of Databricks’ longstanding approach: meeting customers where they are, operating across clouds, and partnering where incentives align.

r002.rationale: It says Databricks started with open-source Spark, but does not state that it sought to make Spark the de facto standard for data processing.

r003.rationale: It describes Databricks as a platform running on cloud infrastructure, but does not say it aimed to be the best place to run Spark.

r004.rationale: It discusses an open data and AI ecosystem and accepting some product overlap, but does not explain prioritizing growth of the Spark ecosystem over avoiding partnerships with potential competitors.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention a substantial engineering commitment required from Databricks for the Microsoft partnership.

astra-6.text:
I think of Microsoft as an important part of a broader strategy: we want to meet customers where they are. If a customer is using Azure, we want to make it easy for them to use Databricks there, and a close partnership with Microsoft helps us do that.

At the same time, we want to work across clouds. Customers have different requirements and existing relationships, so our approach is to give them that choice. These partnerships can involve both cooperation and competition. The key is to focus on where working together creates value for the customer.

r001.rationale: It describes a broader partnership strategy, but does not say the Microsoft partnership continues a longstanding strategy.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Spark or making Spark the de facto standard for data processing.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Spark or differentiating Databricks as the best place to run it.

r004.rationale: It mentions cooperation and competition, but does not explain prioritizing Spark ecosystem growth over avoiding partnerships with competitors.

r005.rationale: It does not mention any substantial engineering commitment by Databricks.

sol-6.1.text:
The Microsoft partnership has been very important for us. With Azure Databricks, we worked closely with Microsoft to deliver an integrated service, so customers can use Databricks as a natural part of Azure. It’s more than simply making our software available on their cloud.

But our broader strategy is to meet customers where they are. Customers have made different cloud choices, and some operate across multiple clouds. We want to support those choices. So we have a deep partnership with Microsoft while also working with other cloud providers. The goal is to make it easier for customers to get value from their data, wherever that data lives.

r002.rationale: It does not mention making Spark the de facto standard for data processing.

r003.rationale: It does not state that Databricks aimed to be the best place to run Spark.
